claims.text: Adding approximately 0.5–1 at% boron to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 will improve its glass-forming ability.
Adding approximately 0.5–1 at% boron will improve the alloy's thermal stability during reheating.
The baseline Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy is produced by arc melting.
Rapid quenching of the baseline alloy produces a largely amorphous structure.
The baseline alloy has limited amorphous retention during reheating.
Boron addition introduces atomic-scale lattice distortion.
Boron addition increases local chemical disorder in the target alloy.
The boron-induced distortion and disorder disrupt nucleation and growth of crystalline phases.
Boron has a smaller atomic size and lower diffusivity than the relevant constituent atoms.
Boron impurities impede the atomic rearrangements required for crystallization.
Suppression of atomic mobility by boron retards devitrification during reheating.
The boron-modified alloy will retain a higher amorphous fraction after rapid solidification than the baseline alloy.
The boron-modified alloy will exhibit a delayed crystallization onset during reheating.
The boron-modified alloy will have a lower crystallization-exotherm temperature during DSC.
The boron-modified alloy will form fewer crystallites during DSC reheating.
The intervention should be effective at melt-spinning cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s.
The intervention should remain effective under moderate DSC reheating protocols.
The benefit of boron may diminish under very slow cooling.
The benefit of boron may diminish under extreme reheating because sufficient thermal energy can overcome the proposed nucleation barriers.
The baseline alloy crystallizes at lower undercooling values than desired, producing a complex thermal response.

contradictions.description: A delayed crystallization onset during a fixed-rate DSC reheating experiment ordinarily implies a higher onset temperature, but the same field predicts a lower crystallization-exotherm temperature.

The falsification rule requires a statistically significant delay in crystallization onset, whereas the predicted outcome also calls for a lower crystallization-exotherm temperature, which would generally indicate earlier rather than delayed crystallization under identical DSC conditions.
